wine.name: L'Ermita
wine.classification: Gran Vinya Classificada of DOQ Priorat, the first so named, from the 2017 vintage
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the great majority, from old bush vines, with a little Cariñena and a few white vines planted among them.
wine.sites: L'Ermita, a steep slope of llicorella facing north east above Gratallops, below the hermitage of Our Lady of Consolation, with bush vines planted before the middle of the twentieth century.
wine.making: Fermented in oak vats, the cap punched down, with a long maceration of about six weeks. Malolactic fermentation and ageing follow in French oak for about a year to a year and a half; the cellar has moved from new barrels towards large oval foudres, used for the 2023 and the 2024.
wine.glass: Black cherry, raspberry and violet over dried thyme, liquorice and slate dust; deep, yet more floral and fresh than its weight suggests, with fine, firm tannin and slate again on the long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after five to ten and lasts two decades and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant it an hour or two before serving if young, gently off its sediment if old; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Catalan for the hermitage: the vineyard takes its name from the chapel on the hill above it.
A great classified vineyard, the rung above Vinya Classificada on Priorat's own ladder; L'Ermita holds it from the 2017 vintage.
Priorat's appellation in Catalan, of the qualified rank that only Rioja shares in Spain.

records.table: Álvaro Palacios takes L'Ermita from one steep slope of old Garnacha on llicorella slate below a hermitage above Gratallops, the first Gran Vinya Classificada of Priorat. Deep yet floral and stony, it is a wine to decant and to pour into a large glass.
records.story: Born into the family of Palacios Remondo, a wine house of Rioja, the founder studied oenology in Bordeaux, working at Pétrus as a student. In 1989, at the invitation of the founder of Clos Mogador, he joined the newcomers gathering at Gratallops, who made their first wines together from that vintage, each sold as a clos; his label was Clos Dofí, the name that passed to the wine of Finca Dofí, his first vineyard. In 1993 he acquired the slope that became L'Ermita: old bush Garnacha on llicorella facing north east, below the hermitage of Our Lady of Consolation, which gave the wine its name, and the first vintage followed that year. Around it he built a ladder of his own, from the regional Camins del Priorat and Les Terrasses through the Gratallops village wine to Finca Dofí and L'Ermita, and the family went on to make wine in Bierzo, at Descendientes de J. Palacios, beside Palacios Remondo in Rioja. Over the years the cellar moved from new barrels towards large oval foudres. In 2019 the denomination presented its ladder of village, site and classified vineyard wines, and L'Ermita was named its first Gran Vinya Classificada, from the 2017 vintage. L'Ermita puts the last rung of Priorat's ladder in one glass: one slope, old Garnacha and slate.

others.name: Finca Dofí

traps: Llicorella is a dark slate shot with quartz, not limestone, and it is the soil of L'Ermita.
Les Terrasses and Camins del Priorat are regional wines of the house, not second wines of L'Ermita.
Priorat is written DOQ in Catalan and DOCa in Castilian, a qualified rank it shares only with Rioja.

report: A search restricted to the house's own domain returned nothing, so the record stands on the DOQ's own pages for the classification and on two secondary sources for each other fact; Wine-Searcher's Q and A and Decanter's Spanish Icons were read through search and not listed for want of room.

The planting of L'Ermita is given as 1900 to 1940, as 1910 and 1940, and as the 1940s, so the record says the first half of the twentieth century; the plot's size differs between sources and is not given.

The élevage is twelve months in oval foudres in one recent account, about eighteen in others, and new barrels for the 2017, so the record says a year to a year and a half, in foudres in recent vintages.
Finca Dofí is dated to 1989 in one source and 1990 in another, so no year is given; Clos Dofí as its first name rests on one merchant and the library.

The technical sheets give between 85 and 92 per cent Garnacha, with a few white vines (named as Garnacha Blanca, Macabeo and Pedro Ximénez in one source only), hence the great majority and no names for the whites.

The Moueix under whom the founder worked at Pétrus differs between sources, and the one named in one of them is living, so neither is named; the founder himself is living and is described, not named, in prose.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, one restricted to the house's domain (empty) and one shared with the group (the DOQ's ladder).

changed: wine.making: was "The bunches are destemmed by hand and the wine is macerated for about six weeks in oak vats, with the cap punched down ... in the 2020s large oval foudres rather than new barrels"; now fermented in oak vats with the cap punched down after about six weeks of maceration, a year to a year and a half in French oak, the cellar moving from new barrels towards oval foudres, used for the 2023 and the 2024: the technical sheets read give part whole bunches for the 2023 and 2024, so hand destemming is not the rule, and one account gives new barrels for the 2022, so the 2020s as a whole cannot be said.

story and questions[1].q: was "In 1993 he bought the slope"; now "acquired": the Rare Wine Co article says he found it in 1993, a merchant that he added it in 1993, and Decanter that he bought it shortly before the first vintage; the year stands, the word follows the sources.
open: The year in which the denomination presented its ladder rests on the date of the DOQ's own leaflet, The Names of the Land, of May 2019, and on a trade news item; no decree was found, so 2019 stays as the year it was presented, not the year it was enacted.

wine.name: Clos Mogador
wine.classification: Vi de Finca Qualificada, by the house's account the first wine in Spain so ranked
wine.grapes: Garnacha leads, with Cariñena, then Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon, in proportions that move with the year.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard around the cellar at Gratallops, which the house calls an immense amphitheatre of llicorella slate; the separate Manyetes parcel makes a wine of its own.
wine.making: The fermentation, on native yeasts alone, takes place in large oak vats or open 300 litre barrels, with a long maceration of four weeks and more. It is then aged in large old oak foudres, with smaller casks beside them in some years, for a year to a year and a half before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, blackberry and wild thyme over hot stone and graphite; full and warm, but savoury rather than sweet, with firm, fine tannin and a dry, stony close.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed for five years or so, it opens slowly, and a strong vintage keeps for twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour or two in a decanter for a young bottle, a gentle decant off the sediment for an old one; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The French word for an enclosed vineyard, which the newcomers of 1989 took for their estate wines.
A single estate rank, as the house describes it: grapes from the estate alone, bottled there.
The denomination, written DOQ in Catalan; Priorat and Rioja alone hold Spain's qualified rank.

records.table: In 1989 the Gratallops estate of Clos Mogador led Priorat's revival: its red is Garnacha and Cariñena, with some Syrah and Cabernet, from its own amphitheatre of llicorella, fermented in oak and aged in large foudres. Warm, dark and savoury, it opens after an hour in a decanter.
records.story: In 1979 a winemaker of a family of French origin, long in the wine trade of Catalonia, bought land at Gratallops with his family: the beginning of Clos Mogador. In 1989 he drew a small group of newcomers to the village, and for the first three vintages, 1989 to 1991, the five pooled their grapes in one rented cellar and sold the one wine under clos labels that settled into five: Clos Mogador, Clos Dofí, Clos Erasmus, Clos Martinet and Clos de l'Obac. The French word clos, an enclosed vineyard, gave each label its first word. From 1992 each house made its own wine, and Clos Mogador went on drawing on the family's vineyard on the llicorella around the cellar, and the house later added Manyetes, from a parcel of Cariñena bottled apart, and a barrel aged white, Nelin. In time the estate gained the rank of Vi de Finca Qualificada, by its own account the first wine in Spain to hold it, a rank that asks for grapes from the estate alone. In later years the house turned from small casks to large old foudres, fermenting with native yeasts alone. Clos Mogador is the founding estate of the five clos, the house where modern Priorat began, and its red is savoury rather than sweet.

others.name: Manyetes
others.note: A wine of its own from the separate Manyetes parcel at Gratallops, led by Cariñena with Garnacha.

others.name: Nelin
others.note: The house's white, led by Garnacha Blanca and aged in barrel; a white, not a second wine of the red.

traps: The five clos of the revival were Mogador, Dofí, Erasmus, Martinet and l'Obac; a later Priorat wine with clos on its label was not one of them.
Nelin is the white of Clos Mogador, not a second wine of the red.
Vi de Finca Qualificada is a single estate rank, not one of the village, site and vineyard rungs that the DOQ presented in 2019.

report: The founder, his wife and their son are living and are described, not named; the founder's name is already in people.json.

The origin of the name Mogador is given three ways (a novel about a family near Avignon, the old name of Essaouira, the vineyard itself) and is left out; so is the claim that the house took the name only in 1997, on one glossary alone.
The year of the Vi de Finca Qualificada is given as 2001 and 2006 in secondary accounts; the house says only that it was the first in Spain, so no year is given and the claim is told as the house's.
The founder's arrival in Priorat is given as 1977, 1978 and 1979; the record keeps the library's 1979 for the land at Gratallops, which the house's pages give too.

The family's French roots are placed at Gigondas in one source and at a domain called Le Martinet in another, and its Penedès firm rests on one glossary, so the story says only a family of French origin long in the Catalan wine trade.

The library's p-clos-mogador calls Nelin the reference for serious white Priorat, a judgement this tab refuses; the record says a barrel aged white. The plan writes Vi de Finca Qualificat; the house and the library write Qualificada.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, two restricted to the house's and the DOQ's domains, and one shared with the group (the five clos of 1989).

changed: wine.grapes: was "Garnacha, about half, with Cariñena, nearly a third"; now Garnacha leads, with Cariñena, then Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon, in proportions that move with the year: the house's own sheet for 2010 gives Garnacha 44 and Cariñena 25 per cent, so neither share holds across vintages; questions[0].exp follows (Garnacha led, not about half).

wine.making and story: the stems are cut ("part of the fruit with its stems", "a share of stems in the vat"): a search of the house's own domain found native yeasts alone and foudres of old wood, but no page on stems; the vintage by vintage cask sizes are folded into large old foudres, with smaller casks in some years, for a year to a year and a half, since the house's pages give a year in 5,000 litre foudres in one place and eighteen months in 2,000 litre foudres in another.

story, traps[0] and wine.label[0].means: the five labels of 1989 become clos labels that settled into five, the five clos of the revival, and clos is the French word for an enclosed vineyard rather than a word taken from Burgundy: Wikipedia and a merchant's history both say the shared wine of 1989 first went out under about ten clos names, and no source read says the word was borrowed from Burgundy.
story: "In time ... In time" becomes "later" for the first, a repeat only.

questions[1].exp: was "2009 the year national law confirmed the DOQ"; now the distractors are simply too late: the DOQ's own pages give the Catalan rank in 2000 and only the state gazette's publication of its rules in 2009, so the claim was loose.
open: The year of the Vi de Finca Qualificada is given as 2001, 2006 and by vintage as 2005 and 2008 across five secondary accounts; several of them say the first in Catalonia or in Priorat rather than in Spain, so the house's claim of Spain stays hedged as its own.

The house's family page tells the origin of the name: Mogador was the name a novelist of the family gave the family's old estate, Le Martinet, in the Vaucluse. It is primary for the house's own account and could stand hedged, but the story is at its cap; left for the integrator.
The same family page says the founder's forebears bottled the first Priorat wines in the 1940s, against Scala Dei's 1878 and the 1974 Cartoixa's claim; see the Scala Dei record.

wine.name: Clos Erasmus
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the larger part, with Syrah for the rest; the share of Syrah moves with the year.
wine.sites: Seventeen terraces, old Garnacha among them, on a hillside just outside Gratallops, on llicorella slate; younger vines and other parcels go to the second wine, Laurel.
wine.making: Picked by hand, then fermented with native yeasts, mostly in oak, with concrete and clay amphorae beside it since the 2010s; the maceration lasts about five weeks. It then spends about a year and a half in French oak barrels, a share of them new, with a little of the wine kept in amphorae.
wine.glass: Kirsch, black cherry and incense over crushed slate and dried thyme; dense and dark, cut by fresh acidity, with fine, firm tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: It needs eight to ten years to open from a dense, closed youth, and lasts well past twenty.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle wants two hours in a decanter, an old one only a gentle decant off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The estate's wine, named for the humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam and his In Praise of Folly.
The denomination, DOQ in Catalan: one of Spain's two denominations of qualified rank, with Rioja.

records.table: On seventeen terraces of llicorella outside Gratallops, Clos Erasmus grows Garnacha with Syrah; the tiny estate was one of the five clos of 1989. Dark and dense, with fresh acidity, incense and crushed slate, it needs a decanter and, before that, years in the cellar.
records.story: Seventeen terraces of vines on a hillside outside Gratallops were the start of Clos Erasmus: its founder, a Swiss newcomer to Priorat, bought them in 1988 and made her first wine with the 1989 vintage, among the five newcomers of the village. For three vintages, 1989 to 1991, the newcomers shared a rented cellar and one pooled wine, and of the clos labels it bore, which came down to five, hers was Clos Erasmus. She named it for the humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam (about 1466 to 1536), an allusion to his In Praise of Folly and an answer to those who called the venture madness. Once the five went their own ways in 1992, hers stayed small: one hillside of terraces, Garnacha led, with Syrah beside it. The company took the name Clos i Terrasses, and the flagship kept the name of Erasmus. Laurel, the second wine, comes from younger vines and other parcels. In the 2010s concrete and clay amphorae joined the oak in the cellar, for a share of the fermentation and a little of the ageing. Examiners usually ask for Clos Erasmus beside L'Ermita when they want the region's classic names: a wine of one terraced hillside, made in small amounts.

The founder is Swiss on the library's word (its trap) and one secondary account; Erasmus's birth year is 1466 or 1469 in the sources, hence about 1466. Scores of a hundred points appear in many accounts and are refused here.

wine.name: Clos Martinet
wine.grapes: Garnacha in most years the larger part, with Cariñena, Syrah and small shares of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, in proportions that move with the year.
wine.sites: Plots of the Mas d'en Martinet estate, which lies in the municipality of Falset but which the house places in the Gratallops wine area, on llicorella slate with many different aspects.
wine.making: Long macerations of about five weeks, part of the fruit with its stems; for the 2022 part of the wine, the Garnacha especially, was made by carbonic maceration and blended back. The wine then ages for about a year in a range of vessels, wood, concrete and clay among them.
wine.glass: Plum, black cherry and liquorice over rosemary and warm slate; full and ripe but fresh, the tannin fine and firm, the finish savoury and stony.
wine.ageing: It opens within a few years of release, then keeps and gains for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter when young; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house, named for its estate, the Mas d'en Martinet; a mas is a Catalan farmhouse with its land.
The flagship red, one of the five clos labels of Priorat's revival, first made in 1989.

records.table: Clos Martinet, first made in 1989 as one of the revival's five clos, comes from Mas Martinet's family estate in the Gratallops wine area: a Garnacha led blend with Syrah and Cariñena on llicorella. Ripe yet fresh, and stony, it should breathe in a decanter for an hour first.
records.story: The family behind Mas Martinet came to Priorat in 1981, according to the house, and spent its first years studying the estate's slopes, rootstocks, grapes, climate and soil before it planted the vineyards that give its wines. The founder was among the handful of newcomers who made the first clos wines together at Gratallops: for the vintages of 1989 to 1991 the group worked from pooled grapes in a single rented cellar, and Clos Martinet was one of the labels it bottled, beside Clos de l'Obac, Clos Dofí, Clos Erasmus and Clos Mogador. From 1992 the five houses worked apart. In 2000, by its own history, the founder's daughter took charge of the estate, and with her came an agroecological approach that treats the vineyards and the land around them as one living whole. Under her the house moved away from the methods of the revival's first years, towards long macerations with stems and a wider range of vessels than the small barrel, and for the 2022 part of the wine went through carbonic maceration. In Clos Martinet the second generation of the revival works on a wine of the first: the same estate and the same clos name, made with a different hand.

traps: Mas Martinet is the house and Clos Martinet its flagship; Martinet Bru is another red of the estate, not the same wine under a second name.
The cellar lies in the municipality of Falset, yet its vineyards belong to the Gratallops wine area of the DOQ.

report: The founder, his wife and his daughter may all be living and none is named; the daughter's name is already in people.json, and the founder's life dates were found in no source, so he is described.

The house's History page gives 1981 for the family's start; other accounts give 1986 for the first wines and 1989 for the estate, so founded is the house's 1981 and the story says by the house's account.
The blend moves widely with the year (one 2021 listing gives Syrah the larger share, another Garnacha), so the record says Garnacha leads in proportions that move with the year.

Native yeasts, eighteen months in barrel and ageing chiefly in foudres with some clay rest on one listing each and are left out; the making says only more than a year in oak and other vessels. The carbonic maceration rests on the 2022 sheets.
The DOQ's own page for the house names the daughter as its winemaker and was read through search, but is not listed for want of room; it agrees with the house on the handover.
No swap proposed: the pick is one of the five clos of 1989 and a sound choice for the region.

Searches for this record: 3 of the group's 35, one restricted to the house's and the DOQ's domains, and one shared with the group (the five clos of 1989). A search of the DOQ's domain for its list of classified vineyards found none of the four houses beside L'Ermita on it, so their classification fields are empty or give only the house's own rank; the group used 26 searches in all.

records.place: Escaladei, La Morera de Montsant, Priorat, Catalonia

wine.name: Scala Dei Cartoixa
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the great majority, with Cariñena for the rest, from old vines.
wine.sites: Old vines on terraces of clay and on steep slopes of slate, at about 400 to 800 metres, in the house's vineyards around Escaladei below the cliffs of the Montsant.
wine.making: Each lot is fermented apart in small cement vats at a controlled temperature, with about three weeks on the skins, as the house describes it. The wine is then aged for about eighteen months before the final blend is bottled.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and dried thyme over fennel and wet slate; fresher and lighter on its feet than the Priorat of the lower villages, with bright acidity and fine tannin, ending on a note of stone.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage, it lasts ten to fifteen years when well kept.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; half an hour or so in a decanter will do for a young bottle; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Catalan for a charterhouse: the Carthusian monastery of Escaladei beside the cellar.
Latin for the ladder of God, the name of the monastery whose priory gave Priorat its name.

records.table: Beside the charterhouse of Escaladei, whose priors named Priorat, Cellers de Scala Dei makes Cartoixa, its old vine red: Garnacha with a little Cariñena from high slopes under the Montsant. First bottled in 1974, it is fresh, red fruited and stony.
records.story: Carthusian monks founded the charterhouse of Santa Maria d'Escaladei at the foot of the Montsant cliffs in the twelfth century, at the wish of the Aragonese crown, the first house of their order in the Iberian Peninsula. The story goes that a shepherd had dreamt of angels climbing a stair to heaven on the spot, and the monks called it Scala Dei, the ladder of God. Its priors ruled the villages around, the Priorat, and planted vines. In 1835 the state's confiscation of church lands drove the monks out, and the buildings fell to ruin. The house dates its origin to 1844, when five families who had bought the monastery's lands founded a company to make wine, and by its account their bottles of Priorat won a gold medal at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878. The cellar was refounded in 1974, and its first Cartoixa, of that vintage, is by several accounts the first wine bottled under the Priorat denomination. By 1990 the owners of the ruined charterhouse had given it to the Generalitat de Catalunya for its recovery, and in 2000 the Codorníu group of Penedès bought into the company. For a sommelier, Cartoixa ties the modern denomination to the monks who named it: Priorat bottled before the revival of 1989.

others.name: Scala Dei Prior
others.note: A younger red of the house, which by its account owes its mineral notes to the llicorella.

others.name: Masdeu
others.note: From the Masdeu vineyard, set above 650 metres on what the house calls a natural balcony over Priorat.

traps: Scala Dei is a place, a cellar and a monastery, not a grape or a style; the priory gave the whole region its name.
Cartoixa is the house's red, named for the charterhouse; the Cartoixa d'Escaladei itself is the monastery, given to the Generalitat by 1990.

report: The monastery's founding is given as 1194 by Wikipedia and 1163 by the Generalitat's heritage page, both at the wish of the same king (Alfonso II of Aragon, Alfons I of Catalonia), so the story says the twelfth century and names no king.

Founded is the house's own 1844, the company of five families it calls its origin; the house also says it was refounded in 1974, and other accounts date the families' purchase to 1840, so the integrator may prefer 1974.

The region record says the house has bottled since the 1970s; the house says its Priorat de Scala-Dei won a gold medal in Paris in 1878, so the story tells both and calls 1974 the first bottling under the denomination, on Spanish Wine Lover and The Drinks Business.
Codorníu's share of 2000 is 25 per cent in two accounts and a controlling stake in the Oxford Companion; the record says only that it bought into the company in 2000.
The departure of 1835 rests on Costa Daurada's tourist pages and Wikipedia; the fire that followed rests on Costa Daurada alone and is left out.

The house gives Cartoixa as 80 per cent Garnacha, a merchant 75; vine age (about 65 years) is volatile and left out. Its own sheets alone stand for the making and the Masdeu vineyard, as the house's own methods.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35.

changed: story and traps[1]: was "In 1991 the house ceded the ruined charterhouse to the Generalitat"; now "By 1990 the owners of the ruined charterhouse had given it to the Generalitat": the Generalitat's heritage pages, a notarial agreement of the Unió de Scala Dei and the Diari de Tarragona give 1990 (one heritage guide 1989), and no source gives 1991.

story: was "its bottles of Priorat de Scala-Dei won a gold medal at the Paris World's Fair of 1878"; now "its bottles of Priorat won a gold medal at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878", in the house's own words on its history page.

wine.making and questions[0]: was each plot fermented apart and each vineyard aged apart "in 500 litre barrels and foudres"; now each lot fermented apart in small cement vats at a controlled temperature, about three weeks on the skins, then about eighteen months before the blend: the house's Cartoixa page gives the vats, the weeks and the months but no vessel for the ageing, and its summary speaks of varieties, not plots.

wine.sites: was "with cooler clay on the higher ground"; now terraces of clay and steep slopes of slate at about 400 to 800 metres: the house says terraces with clay soils and slate slopes, not that the clay lies higher.

table: "beside the ruined charterhouse that named Priorat" becomes "beside the charterhouse of Escaladei, whose priors named Priorat": its church has been restored, and the priors, not the stones, gave the name.
sources[0]: the house's history page is at /en/pages/historia, not /en/pages/history; title and address set right.
open: Three claims of a first bottled Priorat stand side by side: Scala Dei's own of 1878, Clos Mogador's family page of the 1940s, and the 1974 Cartoixa as the first under the denomination's label (The Drinks Business, Spanish Wine Lover, Ara). The record keeps the last, hedged by several accounts.
founded stays the house's 1844, the Sociedad Agrícola La Unión of its history page; the integrator may prefer 1974, the refounding.
